title: Design an LFU cache with O(1) get/put, and extend it with time-based frequency decay and TTL.
shortTitle: Design an LFU cache with O(1) get/put, and extend it with time-based frequency decay and TTL.
topicTitle: Design an LFU cache with O

s1_definition.profdef: An LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache evicts the entry with the lowest access frequency when it is full. Achieving O(1) get and put requires three structures working together: a hash map from key to node, a map from frequency to a doubly linked list of nodes at that frequency (ordered by recency within the same frequency to break ties), and a tracked minimum frequency so the eviction victim is found in constant time. Time-based frequency decay periodically ages old counts so a once-popular key does not dominate forever, and TTL expires entries after a fixed lifetime regardless of frequency.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India caching account balances to avoid hitting the database. An LFU cache keeps the balances that are asked for most often. If the cache is full and a new balance must come in, it throws out the balance that has been requested the fewest times. The frequency decay is like saying "popularity from last year should not count forever," so an account that was hammered during a one-time sale slowly loses its privileged spot. The TTL is the rule that a cached balance is only trusted for, say, thirty seconds, after which it must be refreshed from the ledger no matter how popular it is.
s1_definition.oneliner: An O(1) LFU cache uses a key-to-node map plus frequency-bucketed doubly linked lists with a tracked min frequency, and you layer decay to age old popularity and TTL to expire stale entries.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache evicts the entry with the lowest access frequency when it is full. Achieving O(1) get and put requires three structures working together: a hash map from key to node, a map from frequency to a doubly linked list of nodes at that frequency (ordered by recency within the same frequency to break ties), and a tracked minimum frequency so the eviction victim is found in constant time. Time-based frequency decay periodically ages old counts so a once-popular key does not dominate forever, and TTL expires entries after a fixed lifetime regardless of frequency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India caching account balances to avoid hitting the database. An LFU cache keeps the balances that are asked for most often. If the cache is full and a new balance must come in, it throws out the balance that has been requested the fewest times. The frequency decay is like saying "popularity from last year should not count forever," so an account that was hammered during a one-time sale slowly loses its privileged spot. The TTL is the rule that a cached balance is only trusted for, say, thirty seconds, after which it must be refreshed from the ledger no matter how popular it is.

**One line to remember:** An O(1) LFU cache uses a key-to-node map plus frequency-bucketed doubly linked lists with a tracked min frequency, and you layer decay to age old popularity and TTL to expire stale entries.

sections.s2_technical:
The core data structures are: a `Map<K, Node>` for O(1) lookup, where each node stores the key, value, and its current frequency; a `Map<Integer, DoublyLinkedList>` mapping a frequency to the list of all nodes with that frequency; and an integer `minFreq` tracking the smallest frequency present. Using a doubly linked list per frequency means removing a node from the middle is O(1) because the node holds pointers to its neighbors, and adding to the head is O(1), so ties within a frequency are broken by recency.

On `get(key)`, if the key is missing you return a miss. If present, you read its value, then promote it: remove the node from its current frequency list, increment its frequency, and add it to the head of the next frequency list. If the list you just emptied was the one at minFreq, you increment minFreq. All these steps are O(1). For example after Rajesh's balance is read, its frequency goes from one to two and it moves from bucket one to bucket two.

On `put(key, value)`, if the key exists you update the value and promote it just like a get. If it is new and the cache is at capacity, you evict: look at the list at minFreq, remove its tail (the least recently used among the least frequently used), and delete it from the key map. Then you insert the new node with frequency one, add it to the frequency-one list, and set minFreq to one. This gives O(1) put. Frequency decay is added by periodically halving every node's frequency, or by using a time-aware counter so recent accesses weigh more than old ones; a common production approach, used by Caffeine, is a frequency sketch with periodic aging rather than exact per-key halving, which keeps memory bounded. TTL is added by storing an expiry timestamp on each node and treating an expired node as a miss on access, plus optionally a background sweeper that removes expired nodes. A senior nuance: pure LFU suffers from cache pollution, where a key that was hot long ago never leaves, which is precisely why decay matters, and why real caches like Caffeine use a hybrid of recency and frequency called Window-TinyLFU. Also, in a concurrent banking service you must guard the structure with a lock or use a concurrent cache library, because the multi-step promote and evict operations are not atomic on their own.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India shows account balances constantly, and hitting PostgreSQL for every lookup is slow and expensive. The bank caches balances in memory, but memory is limited, so when the cache fills it must evict something. This is exactly what an LFU cache solves — keep the balances asked for most often and evict the rarely asked ones.

Problem 2 — During a festival sale one account was queried thousands of times in an hour, and afterwards it stayed stuck in the cache forever even though nobody looks at it now. This is exactly what frequency decay solves — old popularity is aged down so stale favorites make room for currently hot accounts.

Problem 3 — A cached balance must never be trusted indefinitely, because the real balance changes. This is exactly what TTL solves — a cached balance expires after a fixed time and is refreshed from the ledger.

The demo implements an O(1) LFU cache with frequency buckets, adds a decay operation and a per-entry TTL, and runs account balance lookups for Rajesh and Priya to show promotion, eviction, decay, and expiry. Classes and steps: `Node`, `DoublyLinkedList`, `LfuCache` (get/put/decay/TTL), and `LfuCacheDemo`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cache of capacity two with a thirty-second TTL, caching Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1,000,000) and Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250,000).

Step 1 — Both balances are put with frequency one, so minFreq is one and both sit in the frequency-one bucket. The key map points to each node directly for O(1) lookup.

Step 2 — Rajesh is read twice and Priya once. Each get removes the node from its bucket, increments its frequency, and adds it to the next bucket's head, all O(1). Rajesh ends at frequency three, Priya at frequency two, and because the frequency-one bucket emptied, minFreq rose.

Step 3 — A new account SAV9999 is put while the cache is full. The cache looks at the minFreq bucket, finds Priya is the least frequently used, removes her tail node in O(1), deletes her from the key map, then inserts SAV9999 at frequency one and resets minFreq to one.

Step 4 — Reading Priya now returns null because she was evicted, while Rajesh is still cached. Then decay halves every frequency so Rajesh drops from three to one, aging his old popularity so he no longer dominates forever, and any entry past its TTL would have been treated as a miss and removed on access.

```
2026-10-26 15:40:01 [INFO] Evicted LFU key=CUR3001 freq=2
2026-10-26 15:40:01 [INFO] Priya after eviction = null
2026-10-26 15:40:01 [INFO] Rajesh still cached   = 1000000
2026-10-26 15:40:01 [INFO] Frequency decay applied; minFreq=1
2026-10-26 15:40:01 [INFO] Rajesh after decay    = 1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  put(SAV2001, 1,000,000) ; put(CUR3001, 250,000)
    keyToNode: {SAV2001→N1, CUR3001→N2}
    freqToList: { 1: [N2(CUR) ⇄ N1(SAV)] }   minFreq=1

  get(SAV2001)×2 , get(CUR3001)×1  (promote: remove → freq++ → add head)
    freqToList: { 2:[N2(CUR,f2)] , 3:[N1(SAV,f3)] }   minFreq=2

  put(SAV9999, 500,000)  [cache full → evict at minFreq=2]
    victim = tail of freqToList[2] = CUR3001 (LFU)  ──► removed
    insert SAV9999 at freq 1
    freqToList: { 1:[N3(SAV9999)] , 3:[N1(SAV)] }    minFreq=1

  get(CUR3001) → null (evicted)   get(SAV2001) → 1,000,000

  decay()  halve all freqs
    SAV9999: 1→1 ; SAV2001: 3→1
    freqToList: { 1:[SAV2001, SAV9999] }   minFreq=1

  TTL: on access, now > expiry → removeNode → treated as miss
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — O(1) LFU Cache Internals ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Two-level indexing: keyToNode + freqToList + minFreq           │
  │    WHY: find victim and promote in O(1), not O(n) scans        │
  │ Sentinel Doubly Linked List: O(1) middle remove / tail evict   │
  │    WHY: break ties by recency within a frequency bucket        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: DoublyLinkedList does list ops; LfuCache does policy        │
  │ O: add decay/TTL without changing core get/put structure       │
  │ D: demo depends on LfuCache API, not its internal maps         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │        LfuCache               │ owns ◆ │  DoublyLinkedList     │
  │ - keyToNode: Map<K,Node>      │───────→│ - head,tail sentinels │
  │ - freqToList: Map<Int,DLL>    │        │ + addToHead(Node)     │
  │ - minFreq: int                │        │ + remove(Node)        │
  │ - capacity, ttlMillis         │        │ + removeTail(): Node  │
  │ + get(K): V        O(1)       │        └──────────────────────┘
  │ + put(K,V): void   O(1)       │ uses ◇ ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ + decay(): void               │───────→│  Node{key,value,freq, │
  │ - promote(Node): void O(1)    │        │       expiry,prev,next}│
  └───────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘

  ── Entry State ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  [FRESH freq1] ──get/put──→ [PROMOTED freqN] ──minFreq evict──→ [EVICTED]
        │                          │ decay halves freq              │
        └── TTL expiry on access ──┴────────────→ [EXPIRED/removed]─┘

  ── Call Chain (get) ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. get(SAV2001) → keyToNode lookup (O(1))
  2.   → if now > expiry → removeNode → return null (TTL)
  3.   → promote: freqList[f].remove → f++ → freqList[f+1].addToHead
  4.   → if emptied minFreq bucket → minFreq++
  5.   → return value
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An LFU cache evicts the least frequently used entry when it is full, and the interesting part of the question is making get and put O(1), because a naive implementation that scans for the minimum frequency is O(n). The trick is three structures working together: a hash map from key to node for constant-time lookup, a map from frequency to a doubly linked list of all nodes at that frequency, and a tracked minimum frequency. The doubly linked list per frequency lets me remove a node from the middle in constant time because the node holds its own neighbor pointers, and it orders nodes by recency so ties within the same frequency are broken least-recently-used first.

On a get I look up the node, read its value, and promote it by removing it from its current frequency list, incrementing its frequency, and adding it to the head of the next list; if I just emptied the list at the minimum frequency I bump the minimum. On a put, if the key is new and the cache is full, I go straight to the minimum-frequency list and evict its tail, which is the least frequently used and, among those, the least recently used, then insert the new node at frequency one and reset the minimum to one. Every step is constant time.

Pure LFU has a well-known flaw called cache pollution, where a key that was extremely hot long ago never leaves because its count stays high forever. That is why I add time-based frequency decay, periodically halving every entry's frequency so old popularity ages out and currently hot keys can take its place. I also add TTL by storing an expiry timestamp on each node and treating an expired entry as a miss on access, with an optional background sweeper, because in banking a cached balance must never be trusted indefinitely since the real balance changes in the ledger.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this is exactly how we cached account balances to take read load off PostgreSQL. The LFU policy kept the most-requested balances hot, the decay stopped a one-time festival spike from pinning an account forever, and the TTL guaranteed every cached balance was refreshed from the ledger within thirty seconds. The senior point I always make is that in a real concurrent service I either guard the whole structure with a lock, because promote and evict are multi-step and not atomic, or, far better, I use a proven library like Caffeine, which implements a hybrid of recency and frequency called Window-TinyLFU with a frequency sketch and periodic aging, giving better hit rates and bounded memory than hand-rolled exact LFU.
